full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractBackground: Severe acute respiratory infections (SARI) remain a major cause of hospitalization and mortality, particularly among children and other vulnerable populations. Early identification of pathogens and disease severity is essential for clinical decision-making. This study evaluated the etiology of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI and the prognostic utility of the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score) in a predominantly pediatric cohort.Methods: In this retrospective study, 117 hospitalized SARS-CoV-2-negative SARI patients, including 103 children and 14 adults, admitted to a tertiary care hospital in North India between September and December 2021 were evaluated. Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), alongside blood and lower respiratory tract cultures. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured. Mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.Results: The median age was 2.0 years (interquartile range, 0.5-7.5 years). Multiplex PCR detected respiratory pathogens in 69.2% of patients, with human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B predominating. Blood cultures were positive in 40/117 patients (34.2%), predominantly yielding methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Overall mortality was 20.5%, increasing to 60% among patients with culture-confirmed sepsis. Elevated CRP and PCT were observed in all septic patients. The ViVI Score showed excellent mortality prediction (area under the curve (AUC) 0.946). A cutoff of ≥30 yielded 83.3% sensitivity and 91.4% specificity and was strongly associated with mortality (OR 53.1, 95% CI 14.5-194.0; p<0.001).Conclusion: HRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen, whereas bacterial sepsis was the principal determinant of mortality. Multiplex molecular diagnostics combined with standardized severity assessment may improve clinical triage, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory pathogen surveillance in resource-limited settings.Keywords: mortality, multiplex pcr, respiratory syncytial virus, sepsis, severe acute respiratory infection, vivi disease severity score
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsStudy design and settingThis retrospective observational study analyzed laboratory and clinical data of patients admitted with severe acute respiratory syndrome during the defined period from September to December 2021, corresponding to the COVID-19 pandemic, at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India. The data analysis was undertaken subsequently in the post-pandemic phase. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of Vardhman Mahavir Medical College and Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India (Approval Ref No. IEC/VMMC/SJH/Cert./05-2024/54, dated 23/07/2024).The primary objective was to establish an etiological profile of pathogens responsible for SARI other than SARS-CoV-2 among hospitalized patients, using a combination of multiplex PCR and conventional microbiological culture. Clinical and laboratory data were retrieved retrospectively from hospital records. The study population was predominantly pediatric, comprising 103 children and 14 adults.Sampling technique and patient selectionConsecutive patients admitted during the study period with signs and symptoms of acute respiratory illness were screened for inclusion. Patients meeting the WHO SARI case definition, with fever ≥38°C and cough, with symptom onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization, were included in the study [1]. The study cohort comprised predominantly pediatric patients, with 103 children and 14 adults.Pathogen detection and laboratory methodsRT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2Nasopharyngeal and/or oropharyngeal swabs were collected from all SARI patients in the hospital during that period and tested for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Patients who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 were included in this study and were subjected to multiplex PCR. Testing was performed in a designated COVID-19 molecular diagnostic laboratory, following Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines [8] and using ICMR-National Institute of Virology-approved commercial RT-PCR kits. The test targeted specific viral genes (e.g., E, ORF) for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA.Multiplex PCR for Respiratory PathogensRespiratory specimens (nasopharyngeal/throat swabs) were further subjected to multiplex PCR using the Fast-Track Diagnostics Respiratory Pathogens 21 Plus (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg). This assay detects Chlamydia pneumoniae, Enterovirus, Haemophilus influenzae B, Human adenovirus, Human bocavirus, Human coronavirus 229E, Human coronavirus HKU1, Human coronavirus NL63, Human coronavirus OC43, Human metapneumoviruses A/B, Human parainfluenza virus 1-4, Human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B, Human rhinovirus, Influenza A virus, Influenza A (H1N1) virus, Influenza B virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Tests were conducted according to the manufacturer's protocol, including appropriate internal and external controls.Conventional Microbiological CultureBlood cultures were performed in all 117 enrolled patients using the BacT/ALERT® automated system (bioMérieux, France). Samples that flagged positive were subcultured on blood and MacConkey agar plates, followed by identification using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Patients with positive blood cultures were clinically evaluated and classified as having sepsis based on the treating clinical team's assessment and documented clinical findings. All 40 patients with positive blood cultures were clinically diagnosed with sepsis. The lower respiratory tract samples were processed using standard microbiological techniques [9,10]. Isolates were identified by morphology, Gram staining, and biochemical profiling.BiomarkersSerum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer were measured on the Mispa i3 automated cartridge-based specific protein analyser (Agappe Diagnostics Ltd., Kerala, India). The platform uses a dual-channel system (rate-based nephelometry and turbidimetry/photometry) and prefilled single-use reagent cartridges with test-specific IC-card (smart card) calibration.Disease severity assessmentThe ViVI Score was used to assess disease severity based on 22 clinical parameters, with a total score ranging from 0 to 48 [11,12]. The scoring was weighted as follows: Disease Severity with Uncomplicated Symptoms (DSU): Weight=1×; Disease Severity with Complicated Symptoms (DSC): Weight=3×; Total Disease Severity Score=DSU + DSC. A schematic representation of the study methodology is shown in Figure 1.Figure 1Schematic representation of the study methodologyFast-Track 21 (Fast-Track Diagnostics, Junglinster, Luxembourg); BacT/ALERT® (bioMérieux, France)PCR: polymerase chain reaction; ET: endotrachealStatistical analysisPathogen distributions and descriptive statistics (median, IQR) were calculated in Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, United States), and odds ratios were estimated using Fisher’s exact test. Diagnostic performance of the ViVI Score for outcome classification was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis of ordinal rating data in JROCFIT v2.0.1 (John Eng; based on ROCFIT by Metz et al.) [13]: outcomes were coded as positive = survival (alive) and negative = death, ViVI scores were converted into an ordinal rating scale in which higher categories represented stronger evidence of the positive state, and a maximum-likelihood unequal-variance binormal ROC model was fitted to estimate the area under the curve (AUC) with its standard deviation; because ViVI is a severity index (higher scores indicate poorer prognosis), the ratings were oriented such that lower ViVI scores corresponded to stronger evidence of survival.

full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThe present study provides a comprehensive etiological and clinical profile of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in a predominantly pediatric cohort, with simultaneous assessment of respiratory pathogens, bacterial culture results, inflammatory biomarkers, and disease severity. Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, while HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen. Culture-confirmed bloodstream infection was associated with substantially higher mortality, and the ViVI Score demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality.The 69.2% pathogen detection rate observed with multiplex PCR is consistent with previous studies demonstrating substantial pathogen detection among patients with severe respiratory infection. El Kholy et al. reported a high rate of viral detection and frequent co-detection in children with SARI, while Contier et al. demonstrated the diagnostic performance of multiplex PCR among critically ill immunocompromised patients [14,15]. Differences in age distribution, disease severity, sampling practices, seasonality, and the respiratory pathogen panels used may account for variations in diagnostic yield between studies.HRSV A/B was the predominant respiratory pathogen in our cohort. This finding is consistent with surveillance studies from different geographical settings, including Senegal, India, and Suriname, which have identified HRSV as an important cause of severe respiratory illness and hospitalization among children [16-18]. The global burden of HRSV is substantial. A systematic analysis estimated 33.0 million HRSV-associated acute lower respiratory infection episodes, 3.6 million hospital admissions, and 101,400 deaths among children younger than five years in 2019, with the majority of deaths occurring in low- and middle-income countries [19].The frequency of co-infections observed in our cohort is also consistent with previous pediatric SARI studies using multiplex molecular platforms. Lamrani Hanchi et al. reported pathogen detection in 72.5% of hospitalized children and co-infection in 23.3%, highlighting the ability of multiplex PCR to identify multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen [20]. Similarly, studies incorporating digital surveillance and virological characterization have emphasized the value of combining pathogen detection with standardized clinical information [21,22]. These findings support the use of syndromic molecular testing as an adjunct to conventional microbiological investigations in patients with severe respiratory disease. However, detection of a respiratory pathogen does not necessarily establish causality, particularly for respiratory viruses that may be detected during prolonged shedding or asymptomatic infection. Therefore, multiplex PCR results should be interpreted in conjunction with clinical findings, disease severity, and conventional microbiological results.The exceptionally high mortality observed among SARI patients with culture-confirmed sepsis (60%) was substantially higher than the overall mortality in the cohort. This finding is consistent with pediatric intensive-care data demonstrating significant mortality among children with bloodstream-infection-associated severe sepsis [23]. The finding emphasizes the importance of early recognition of bacterial superinfection and sepsis among patients presenting with severe respiratory illness, particularly when clinical deterioration or evidence of systemic infection is present.HRSV-associated disease severity is influenced by age and underlying clinical conditions. Recent multicenter pediatric data have demonstrated increased risk of severe RSV disease among younger children, premature infants, and older children with pulmonary or neurological, neuromuscular, or developmental conditions [24]. In our cohort, children with underlying hematological disorders represented an important high-risk subgroup, and HRSV-associated ARDS was associated with severe clinical outcomes. These findings reinforce the importance of identifying underlying risk factors when assessing patients with HRSV-associated SARI.The ViVI Score provided a structured approach to clinical severity assessment. Previous work has emphasized the importance of standardized severity assessment for respiratory viral illness and SARI [5]. More recent severity scales have also been evaluated to support respiratory hospitalization surveillance and viral genomic surveillance [25]. In our cohort, a ViVI score of ≥30 demonstrated excellent discrimination for mortality, with an AUC of 0.946. This finding supports the potential utility of standardized severity assessment for identifying patients at increased risk of poor outcomes. However, prospective validation in independent populations is required before this threshold can be considered for broader clinical implementation.Raised PCT and CRP concentrations were associated with culture-positive sepsis and adverse clinical outcomes in our cohort. Previous pediatric data have evaluated PCT and CRP as markers of sepsis, with PCT potentially providing useful information regarding bacterial infection and disease severity [26]. However, neither biomarker should be interpreted as a stand-alone diagnostic test. Their value is greatest when interpreted together with the clinical presentation, microbiological findings, and other laboratory parameters.The findings also have implications for respiratory disease surveillance and clinical triage. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment can provide information on both pathogen circulation and clinical severity [21,22,25]. Such an approach may be particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings, where molecular diagnostic capacity is concentrated at tertiary-care facilities, and timely referral of patients with severe disease remains important. In primary-care settings, recognition of clinical warning signs and timely referral remain essential, while tertiary-care molecular testing can provide additional etiological information.The post-pandemic period is particularly relevant for respiratory pathogen surveillance because changes in population immunity, non-pharmaceutical interventions, and patterns of viral circulation may influence the timing and intensity of respiratory virus activity [16]. Continued surveillance is therefore important for identifying changing epidemiological patterns, detecting populations at increased risk of severe disease, and informing healthcare preparedness.The predominance of HRSV in our cohort also highlights the importance of preventive strategies. Current approaches to prevention of severe RSV disease include maternal vaccination and long-acting monoclonal antibody strategies, particularly for infants at greatest risk of severe disease [27]. Continued pathogen-specific surveillance will be important for evaluating the epidemiological impact of these interventions.The study has several strengths. It integrates multiplex molecular diagnostics with conventional microbiological culture, inflammatory biomarkers, and standardized severity assessment, allowing simultaneous evaluation of pathogen distribution, bacterial superinfection, disease severity, and mortality. The use of a standardized severity score also enabled quantitative assessment of the relationship between clinical severity and mortality.In this study, several limitations should nevertheless be considered. The retrospective single-center design and relatively small sample size limit generalizability. The cohort was predominantly pediatric (103 children and 14 adults), which reflects the population evaluated at our center during the study period. Consequently, the findings, particularly those related to pathogen distribution, disease severity, and mortality risk stratification, should be interpreted primarily in the context of pediatric SARI and may not be directly generalizable to adult SARI populations. full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsHRSV was the predominant respiratory pathogen identified among hospitalized patients with non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI. Multiplex molecular testing provided useful etiological information, while the ViVI Score demonstrated good discriminatory ability for mortality risk in this cohort. Further prospective studies in larger and more diverse populations are needed to validate these findings.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionSevere acute respiratory infections (SARI) pose a significant global health challenge, causing substantial morbidity and mortality, particularly among vulnerable populations. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines SARI as an acute respiratory illness with a history of fever or measured fever of ≥38°C and cough, with onset within the last 10 days, requiring hospitalization [1]. However, this syndromic definition does not provide information regarding the underlying etiological agent or the individual risk of adverse outcomes. SARI may result from a wide range of viral and bacterial pathogens, and conventional diagnostic methods may not always provide a timely or comprehensive etiological diagnosis.Before the COVID-19 pandemic, SARI detection was largely syndromic, relying on clinical presentation and limited diagnostic capacity [2]. The pandemic acted as a catalyst for strengthening surveillance systems and pathogen identification. In India, surveillance of epidemic-prone diseases is supported through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme, including laboratory-based and information technology-enabled surveillance [3].SARI constitutes a major cause of healthcare utilization and hospitalization and may require referral to secondary and tertiary healthcare facilities, particularly among young children, older adults, and individuals with underlying comorbidities. Family physicians are often the first point of contact for patients presenting with acute respiratory symptoms and therefore play a pivotal role in early recognition of severe disease, timely referral, initiation of appropriate management, and implementation of infection prevention measures [1,2]. Accurate identification of respiratory pathogens and early risk stratification are essential to improve patient outcomes while minimizing unnecessary antibiotic use [2].In low- and middle-income countries such as India, access to specialized diagnostic services remains limited at primary-care facilities, with sample transport and referral mechanisms used to improve access to diagnostic testing [4]. Consequently, evidence on the etiological profile of SARI and validated clinical severity assessment tools is highly relevant for strengthening referral pathways, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory disease surveillance. Such evidence can assist family physicians and primary care providers in identifying patients requiring urgent referral, promoting rational antimicrobial use, and optimizing utilization of healthcare resources [2,4].To standardize clinical assessment, various severity scoring systems have been introduced. One of the most widely recognized is the ViVI Disease Severity Score (ViVI Score), developed by the Vienna Vaccine Safety Initiative. This 22-item composite score quantifies the clinical severity of influenza-like illnesses and SARI across diverse patient populations [5]. It includes indicators of both uncomplicated and complicated disease, providing a standardized framework for clinical decision-making, disease severity assessment, and epidemiological comparison.The advent of multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) platforms has markedly advanced the diagnostic approach to SARI by enabling simultaneous detection of multiple respiratory pathogens from a single clinical specimen, thereby improving diagnostic accuracy and expediting clinical decision-making [6]. Integration of rapid molecular diagnostics with standardized severity assessment has the potential to improve clinical risk stratification while strengthening pathogen-specific surveillance and facilitating the integration of virological and clinical data for surveillance and public health applications [6,7].Despite advances in molecular diagnostics and standardized severity assessment, evidence integrating pathogen identification with clinical risk stratification in non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI remains limited, particularly from resource-constrained settings. Addressing this gap may help strengthen clinical decision-making, antimicrobial stewardship, and respiratory infection surveillance across primary and tertiary healthcare settings. title_original: Molecular Etiology and Mortality Risk Stratification of Non-SARS-CoV-2 Severe Acute Respiratory Infection in a Predominantly Pediatric Cohort: A Retrospective Study From a Tertiary Care Hospital in North India

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify the etiological profile of pathogens causing severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) other than SARS-CoV-2 in a pediatric cohort during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting the need to understand non-SARS-CoV-2 causes of SARI in hospitalized children.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This retrospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary care teaching hospital in North India from September to December 2021, focusing on hospitalized patients with SARI who tested negative for SARS-CoV-2. The study population included 103 children and 14 adults, with a male-to-female ratio of 1.81:1.
analysis.methods: Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) alongside blood and lower respiratory tract cultures. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin (PCT), and D-dimer levels were measured, and mortality prediction was assessed using the ViVI Score and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis.
analysis.main_results: Multiplex PCR detected at least one respiratory pathogen in 69.2% of patients, with human respiratory syncytial virus (HRSV) A/B being the most frequently identified. No cases of human metapneumovirus were detected, and other pathogens such as Chlamydophila pneumoniae, enterovirus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae were also not found.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study highlights the predominance of HRSV in non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI cases among hospitalized children, while also noting the absence of human metapneumovirus detection. This suggests that HRSV may be a more significant pathogen in this context than human metapneumovirus.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the etiology of non-SARS-CoV-2 SARI in pediatric populations, which can inform targeted surveillance and diagnostic strategies in resource-limited settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias, as it relied on existing clinical data. The evidence for human metapneumovirus absence is based on the lack of detection in the tested cohort, which may not fully represent all possible cases.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective observational study conducted at a tertiary care hospital in North India from September to December 2021 aimed to determine the etiological profile of severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) in hospitalized children, excluding SARS-CoV-2. The study population included 103 children and 14 adults, with a male predominance. Respiratory pathogens were identified using multiplex PCR and cultures, alongside measuring inflammatory markers. Multiplex PCR detected at least one pathogen in 69.2% of patients, with HRSV A/B being the most common. No human metapneumovirus cases were identified, and other pathogens were also absent. The study suggests HRSV may be a more significant cause of SARI in this cohort than human metapneumovirus. The findings have implications for improving surveillance and diagnostics in pediatric populations, particularly in resource-limited settings. However, the study's retrospective nature and potential selection bias limit its generalizability and confidence in the absence of human metapneumovirus detection.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify the etiological profile of pathogens causing severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) other than SARS-CoV-2 in a pediatric cohort during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting the need to understand non-SARS-CoV-2 causes of SARI in hospitalized children.
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本回顾性观察性研究于2021年9月至12月期间在北印度一家三级教学医院进行,聚焦于SARS-CoV-2检测阴性的SARI住院患者。研究人群包括103名儿童和14名成人,男女比例为1.81:1。
elements_zh.methods: 通过多重聚合酶链反应(PCR)结合血液和下呼吸道培养来识别呼吸道病原体。测量了血清C反应蛋白(CRP)、降钙素原(PCT)和D-二聚体水平,并使用ViVI评分和受试者工作特征(ROC)曲线分析评估死亡率预测。
elements_zh.main_results: 多重PCR检测到至少一种呼吸道病原体的患者占69.2%,其中人呼吸道合胞病毒(HRSV)A/B是最常见的病原体。未检测到人偏肺病毒病例,其他病原体如沙眼衣原体肺炎、肠道病毒和肺炎支原体也未被发现。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 本研究突显了HRSV在非SARS-CoV-2 SARI住院儿童中的主导地位,同时指出未检测到人偏肺病毒。这表明HRSV可能比人偏肺病毒在该背景下更为重要。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果为了解非SARS-CoV-2 SARI在儿童群体中的病因提供了见解,有助于在资源有限的环境中制定针对性的监测和诊断策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于其回顾性设计,可能存在选择偏倚,因为其依赖于现有的临床数据。对于人偏肺病毒缺失的证据是基于在所测试的队列研究中未检测到该病原体,这可能无法完全代表所有可能的病例。

title: Clinical characteristics and exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis

full_text: AbstractObjectiveThe aim of this study was to describe the clinical characteristics of severe viral encephalitis (SVE) in children and to identify exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality, thereby providing preliminary evidence to facilitate early risk stratification and reduce SVE-related disability and mortality.MethodsA retrospective study was conducted in 75 children diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital, from January 2023 to December 2025, including 50 mild cases and 25 SVE cases. Demographic data, clinical manifestations, and laboratory parameters (peripheral white blood cell count (WBC), serum sodium, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leukocyte and protein levels, serum neuron-specific enolase (NSE), electroencephalography (EEG), neuroimaging findings, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores) were collected and compared between groups. Pathogen detection was conducted through multiplex PCR and/or serum viral IgM antibody testing. In the mild encephalitis group, 14 out of 50 cases (28%) were found to be infected with specific viruses, with enteroviruses (EVs) being the predominant type, accounting for 7 cases, followed by herpes zoster virus (VZV) and human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6), each with 2 cases. In the SVE group, 9 out of 25 cases (36%) were found to have pathogens, with influenza A virus (4 cases) and herpes simplex virus (2 cases) being the main ones. Univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to explore factors associated with in-hospital mortality (primary outcome) within the SVE subgroup.ResultsAmong the 25 children with SVE (15 males, mean age 7.74 ± 2.2 years), fever (76%), signs of elevated intracranial pressure (68%), and seizures (56%) were common; four patients died (16%). Compared with children with mild encephalitis, the SVE group exhibited significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, higher proportions of abnormal EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, and elevated serum NSE (all P < 0.05). However, there were no significant differences in CSF leukocytes, CSF protein, blood leukocytes, or serum sodium. In univariate Firth-corrected logistic regression, neuroimaging abnormalities (P = 0.007), seizures (P = 0.011), EEG abnormalities (P = 0.018), lower GCS score (per 1-point decrease, P < 0.001), and higher serum NSE (per 10 ng/mL increment, P = 0.018) were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality.ConclusionPediatric SVE presents with nonspecific early symptoms and substantial mortality. Seizures, EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, low GCS score, and elevated serum NSE are exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality. However, given the small sample size and single-center design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multi-center prospective cohorts. Early recognition of these factors may aid in clinical risk assessment.Keywords: children, clinical characteristics, exploratory factors, in-hospital mortality, severe viral encephalitis 2.Subjects and methods2.1.Study subjectsAll cases were derived from pediatric inpatients diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital from January 2023 to December 2025. All enrolled children fulfilled comprehensive diagnostic criteria for viral encephalitis as follows: (1) Acute onset of neurological symptoms and signs; (2) CSF examination showing an elevated WBC count (> 10 × 106/L) with a predominance of lymphocytes, and/or a mild increase in protein; (3) Electroencephalogram and/or cranial imaging showing changes consistent with viral encephalitis; (4) Other central nervous system diseases such as purulent meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, and autoimmune encephalitis were excluded. Alternative central nervous system infections were excluded according to the following criteria: 1) Bacterial purulent meningitis: excluded based on CSF profiles (predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes, low glucose, elevated protein), negative bacterial culture, and absence of clinical response to empirical antibiotic therapy. 2) Tuberculous meningitis: Excluded by CSF findings (lymphocytic pleocytosis, markedly elevated protein, decreased glucose), negative Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and clinical response to antiviral therapy rather than anti-tuberculous therapy. 3) Cryptococcal meningitis: Excluded by negative India ink stain and negative cryptococcal antigen test in CSF. 4) Autoimmune encephalitis: Excluded by negative testing for anti-neuronal antibodies (anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2, anti-GAD) in both serum and CSF.In terms of pathogen detection, all children provided blood and CSF samples that were tested using multiplex PCR method or serum virus IgM antibody detection to detect viruses: herpes simplex virus 1/2 type, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), human herpesvirus 6 type; at the same time, throat swabs were collected for respiratory virus PCR detection (including influenza virus A/B, human parainfluenza virus, SARS-CoV-2). Pathogen detection in CSF and blood was performed using the Multiplex PCR Kit (Anhui Ranchi Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China), which detects HSV-1/2, VZV, and HHV-6. Respiratory viruses were detected from throat swabs using the Respiratory Virus PCR Kit (Guojun Group Anqing Co., Ltd., China), which includes influenza A/B, human parainfluenza virus, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and SARS-CoV-2. Serum virus-specific IgM antibodies were measured using commercial ELISA kits (Hefei Anmeson Medical Devices Co., Ltd., China). Notably, pathogen detection rates are influenced by multiple factors, including sampling timing, viral load, and primer design. A negative pathogen assay result does not exclude a clinical diagnosis of viral encephalitis (9). In cases where pathogen testing was negative, a clinical diagnosis of viral encephalitis was accepted based on the comprehensive criteria described above (acute neurological symptoms, CSF pleocytosis with lymphocytic predominance, compatible EEG/neuroimaging findings, and exclusion of other CNS diseases).The patients were divided into two groups: a mild viral encephalitis group (n = 50) and an SVE group (n = 25). All patients met the diagnostic criteria for pediatric severe viral encephalitis as defined by a practical review on diagnostic approach and treatment. The diagnostic criteria for mild viral encephalitis were based on reference (10): All of the following clinical features must be met: 1) Consciousness state: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≥ 13 points (drowsy or agitated, but able to be awakened, and able to follow commands); 2) Seizure episodes: No seizures, or only single, brief convulsive episodes; 3) Focal signs: No obvious limb paralysis, cranial nerve palsy, or ataxia (or extremely mild and short-term recovery); 4) Intracranial hypertension: No severe headache, projectile vomiting, papilledema, and normal fundus examination; 5) Vital signs: Stable respiration, heart rate, and blood pressure, no need for ventilator support; 6) Daily abilities: Can eat independently, with basic life skills retained. The diagnostic criteria for SVE were adopted without modification from reference (7) and included at least one of the following conditions: (1) Frequent convulsions or status epilepticus; (2) Consciousness disturbance with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score < 8; (3) Limb paralysis or neurobehavioral abnormalities; (4) Brainstem symptoms; (5) Severe or persistent intracranial hypertension; (6) Multiple organ impairment progressing to failure. Because seizures and low GCS are components of the SVE definition, their associations with mortality within the SVE subgroup should be interpreted as severity markers rather than independent predictors. This study was approved by the ethics committee of Anqing Municipal Hospital (2024-94).Grouping based on GCS and seizures introduces definition-dependent differences between mild and severe cases; thus, comparisons serve only to describe clinical profiles, not to validate diagnostic values. In the prognostic regression analysis, whose primary outcome is in-hospital mortality within the SVE group, these variables are included as potential exploratory factors. However, because seizures and low GCS are components of the SVE definition, their association with mortality should be interpreted with caution, as discussed in the discussion section. Discharge-level functional prognosis was evaluated using the Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS): 1 = death, 2 = persistent vegetative state, 3 = severe disability, 4 = moderate disability, 5 = good recovery. Poor outcome was defined as GOS 1–3, whereas favorable outcome corresponded to GOS 4–5. GOS was collected for descriptive functional-status summarization and was not adopted as the primary endpoint in prognostic regression models.2.2.Data collectionEarly indicators were collected from children with viral encephalitis within 24–48 h after admission, as described below. All variables included in the prognostic regression analysis were measured at admission or within 24 h of admission, prior to knowledge of the clinical outcome.2.2.1.Clinical symptoms and signs (assessed at admission or within 24 h after admission)1) Level of consciousness: The adapted Pediatric Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score (11)—a core indicator of neurological function. A GCS score ≤ 12 or a rapid decline in GCS suggests severe disease. All assessors were pediatric critical-care specialists of attending-physician rank or higher. Pediatric GCS scores were independently assigned and cross-validated by two assessors (physicians and nurses). All assessors had passed the standardized training and assessment within the department. The results of the two assessments were consistent (with a total score difference of ≤ 1 point), and the results are reliable. 2) Seizure manifestations: Presence of convulsive status epilepticus, frequent seizures (≥ 3 episodes within 24 h); or focal seizures suggesting damage to a specific brain region. 3) Signs of increased intracranial pressure: Vomiting (especially projectile); bulging anterior fontanel (in infants). 4) Motor dysfunction: Hemiplegia or significant abnormalities in muscle tone (hypertonia or hypotonia). 5) Systemic manifestations: Hyperthermia (e.g., body temperature > 39 °C or difficult-to-control fever); hypothermia (may indicate severe sepsis or brainstem damage).2.2.2.Routine laboratory indicators (initial test results)1) Peripheral blood test: White blood cell (WBC) count—a significantly elevated or decreased count may indicate severe disease. 2) Serum sodium: hyponatremia, especially < 130 mmol/L, strongly suggests possible syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), which is a marker of increased intracranial pressure and disease worsening. 3) Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis: WBC count—a high count does not necessarily indicate more severe disease; Protein content—a significant elevation (> 1 g/L) indicates severe disruption of the blood-brain barrier.2.2.3.Biomarkers of neurological injurySerum neuron-specific enolase (NSE), which reflects neuronal injury. Within one hour of the patient's admission, blood samples were collected for testing (Shanghai Fudai Testing Technology Group Co. Ltd.). The double-antibody sandwich chemiluminescence immunoassay method was used. The laboratory reference range for serum NSE in healthy children in our institution is 0–16.3 ng/mL. A threshold of > 25.0 ng/mL was predefined by the manufacturer and supported by previous literature as indicating clinically significant neuronal injury, and was used to define “elevated” NSE in the descriptive analyses. For the regression analysis, serum NSE was modeled as a continuous variable per 10 ng/mL increment.2.2.4.Early imaging and neurophysiological examinations (performed within 24 h)1) Neuroimaging: Neuroimaging was performed in all 75 enrolled patients. Cranial MRI was performed in 22 SVE patients and 45 mild VE patients; 3 SVE patients underwent CT because of their clinical condition. MRI abnormalities were defined as single or multiple abnormal signal intensities on T1- and T2-weighted sequences, with or without contrast enhancement. CT abnormalities were defined as focal or diffuse hypodensities or cerebral edema. To maintain analytical consistency in the analysis, “neuroimaging abnormalities” included findings from either MRI or CT. 2) Electroencephalography (EEG): A 30-minute monitoring session was performed. Abnormal EEG findings included widespread theta or delta slow waves (< 4 Hz), persistent asymmetry in wave amplitudes on both sides (one side decreased > 50% or increased > 100%), loss of reactivity, sharp waves, spike waves: sharp-slow or spike-slow complex waves were considered abnormal.2.3.Statistical analysisStatistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 20.0. Normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Continuous variables with a normal distribution were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and inter-group comparisons were performed using the independent-samples t-test. Non-normally distributed continuous variables were expressed as median with interquartile range [IQR], and inter-group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables were expressed as frequency (n) and percentage (%), and comparisons were performed using the chi-square test or Fisher's exact test. Univariate analysis was performed to identify exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE. Univariate logistic regression with Firth's penalized-likelihood estimation was implemented for bias correction. All statistical tests were two-tailed, and P < 0.05 was regarded as the threshold for statistical significance.The statistical analysis was conducted in two distinct parts. First, descriptive comparisons of demographic, clinical, and laboratory characteristics were performed between the mild encephalitis and SVE groups to illustrate the clinical profile of SVE (Tables 1, 2). Second, a prognostic analysis was performed exclusively within the SVE subgroup (n = 25), using univariate Firth-penalized logistic regression to explore factors associated with the primary outcome of in-hospital mortality (Table 3). The variables included in the regression models were pre-specified as age, sex, GCS score, presence of seizures, EEG abnormalities, neuroimaging abnormalities, and serum NSE levels.Table 1Demographic and Clinical Characteristics of Children with Mild and Severe Viral Encephalitis.VariableMild viral encephalitis (n = 50)Severe viral encephalitis (n = 25)P-valueDemographicAge (years), mean ± SD5.80 ± 2.207.74 ± 2.20<0.01Male, n (%)27 (54.00)15 (60.00)0.62Season (Winter-Spring), n (%)21 (42.00)17 (68.00)0.03Prior Health Status, n (%)47 (94.00)24 (96.00)0.72Clinical PresentationLength of hospitalization (d), mean ± SD9.68 ± 3.0913.28 ± 4.82<0.01Length of fever (d), mean ± SD2.24 ± 2.513.12 ± 2.650.16GCS score, mean ± SD14.22 ± 0.919.96 ± 3.07<0.01Seizures, n (%)14 (28.00)14 (56.00)0.02Fever, n (%)40 (80.00)19 (76.00)0.69Table 2Comparison of laboratory indicators between children with SVE and those with mild viral encephalitis.VariableMild viral encephalitis (n = 50)Severe viral encephalitis (n = 25)P-valueEEG abnormalities, n (%)20 (40.0)21 (84.0)<0.01Neuroimaging abnormalities, n (%)8 (16.0)11 (44.0)<0.01CSF leukocyte count (×106/L), median [IQR]26 [8–87]68 [12–134]0.16CSF protein (mg/L), median [IQR]247 [146–580]982 [354–1,326]0.21Peripheral blood WBC (×109/L), mean ± SD12.56 ± 17.709.39 ± 4.130.38Serum sodium (mmol/L), mean ± SD137.41 ± 5.56136.62 ± 4.130.53Serum NSE (ng/mL), median [IQR]37 [16–49]48 [30–84]<0.01Data are presented as mean ± SD, median [IQR], or n (%). Mild cases occurred year-round; 21 (42%) presented in winter-spring (December-May) and 29 (58%) in summer-autumn (June-November). Among the 25 SVE patients, there were 15 males and 10 females, with a mean age of 7.74 ± 2.2 years. SVE also occurred throughout the year, with 17 cases (68%) in winter-spring and 8 cases (32%) in summer-autumn. Acute onset (≤ 7 days) was observed in 23 cases (92%), and subacute onset (> 7 days) in 2 cases (8%). Compared with the mild viral encephalitis group, the SVE group had significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates and lower GCS scores (all P < 0.05), while the incidence of fever was not significantly different between the two groups (P > 0.05). See Table 1.All 75 children (50 mild, 25 SVE) underwent blood and CSF sampling for pathogen detection using multiplex PCR and/or serum virus IgM antibody tests. Additionally, throat swabs for respiratory virus PCR were collected for all patients. In the mild encephalitis group, 14 out of 50 cases (28%) were found to be infected with specific viruses. Among them, 7 cases were infected with enteroviruses (EVs), followed by VZV and human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6), each with 2 cases; 1 case of influenza A virus; 1 case of parainfluenza virus; and 1 case of EBV. Among the 25 SVE patients, 4 were infected with influenza A, 2 with HSV, 1 with SARS-CoV-2, 1 with human parainfluenza, 1 with adenovirus, and the remaining cases had no specific virus identified (clinical diagnosis was accepted as per the criteria described in Methods).3.2.Clinical symptoms and signs (SVE)Fever was the most frequent clinical symptom, observed in 19 out of 25 patients (76%), followed by signs of elevated intracranial pressure (e.g., headache and vomiting) in 17 patients (68%). Neurological dysfunction, including limb shaking, unsteady gait, hemiplegia, or slurred speech, was the initial manifestation in 8 patients (32%). Respiratory symptoms occurred during the disease course in 15 patients (60%). Psychobehavioral abnormalities, mainly excitatory symptoms such as irritability and delirium, were present in 6 patients (24%). Altered consciousness was observed in 11 patients (44%), and cognitive impairment was noted in a small proportion of cases (8%). Seizures occurred in 14 patients, predominantly as generalized seizures.3.3.Comparison of laboratory indicators between pediatric SVE and mild viral encephalitisCompared with the mild viral encephalitis group, the SVE group had significantly longer hospital stays, higher rates of seizures, and lower GCS scores (all P < 0.05). Regarding laboratory indicators, the SVE group showed significantly higher rates of EEG abnormalities, neuroimaging abnormalities, and serum NSE levels than the mild encephalitis group (all P < 0.05). Among the 25 patients with SVE, 22 underwent cranial MRI and 3 underwent cranial CT because of their clinical condition. Eleven patients (44%) had abnormal neuroimaging findings: 10 on MRI and 1 on CT. MRI abnormalities presented as single or multiple patchy or band-like long T1 and long T2 signals, and some were accompanied by inflammatory demyelination. The MRI lesions involved the unilateral insular lobe in 4 cases, the brainstem in 2, the cerebellum in 1, the bilateral frontal lobes in 4, and extensive brain parenchyma in 2. EEG was abnormal in 21 cases: 11 showed paroxysmal diffuse high-amplitude slow waves, and 10 had focal epileptic discharges. However, no significant differences were observed in CSF leukocyte count, CSF protein, blood leukocyte count, or serum sodium (all P > 0.05). See Table 2.3.4.Univariate comparisons and firth-penalized logistic regression for factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVEThe primary outcome for this analysis was in-hospital mortality (death versus survival during hospitalization). Among continuous variables, the death group had significantly lower GCS scores (P = 0.001) and significantly higher serum NSE levels (P = 0.007) compared with the survival group. Similarly, each 10 ng/mL increment in serum NSE was associated with an increased in-hospital mortality risk (P = 0.018). The odds ratio for GCS is interpreted per 1-point decrease in the score (lower GCS → higher mortality risk). The odds ratio for NSE is interpreted per 10 ng/mL increment. No significant associations were found for length of fever, CSF leukocyte count, CSF protein, peripheral blood WBC count, or serum sodium (all P > 0.10). full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionViral encephalitis arises from viral invasion of the intracranial compartment, triggering diffuse parenchymal brain inflammation. Early clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and may be limited to non-specific symptoms including fever, headache, fatigue, and myalgia (12). The incidence of viral encephalitis shows a seasonal pattern, with peaks from June to July and from December to January (13), which is similar to the pattern observed in this study. The winter-spring predominance in our cohort may reflect the circulation pattern of respiratory viruses such as influenza and adenovirus, which constituted the majority of identified pathogens in this study. Unlike the classic predominance of enteroviruses reported in other pediatric encephalitis cohorts (14), our findings suggest that respiratory viruses may play a more prominent role in severe encephalitis cases during the winter-spring season in our region. Furthermore, we found that the age of children with severe encephalitis in Anqing was slightly older than that of those with mild conditions. In the present cohort, the pathogen detection rate among patients with SVE reached 36% (9/25). Influenza-A virus was the most frequently identified pathogen (4/25, 16%), followed by herpes simplex virus (2/25, 8%). This distribution was different from the classic pattern reported in the literature. It is possible that during this period, the enterovirus may not be the predominant circulating strain in this region. The sensitivity of viral nucleic acid testing is influenced by various factors such as sampling time, primer design, and viral load, approximately 40% to 60% of clinical cases of viral encephalitis have no identifiable pathogen, as documented in the literature (14).In recent years, the onset of viral encephalitis has shown a trend toward younger age groups, with increased incidence in neonates and infants (15). If not diagnosed and treated promptly, children may develop severe neurological complications (16); therefore, early and accurate diagnosis is crucial for improving prognosis. In most cases, mild viral encephalitis has a good prognosis after active treatment, whereas severe viral encephalitis progresses rapidly, is more likely to cause other CNS symptoms, leads to sequelae, and can even result in death (7). Clinically, brain failure is common in severe viral encephalitis and is an important cause of death in pediatric intensive care units. In the acute phase of pediatric SVE, various symptoms may occur, including agitation, drowsiness, coma, neurological dysfunction, convulsions, and psychobehavioral abnormalities. The most common clinical symptoms of SVE are headache, decreased consciousness, and convulsions, and in most cases the viral etiology remains unknown (3, 12), which is consistent with the clinical presentation of SVE patients in this study. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a rapid indicator of the severity of brain injury and plays an important role in determining patient prognosis. In the present study, univariate analyses demonstrated that children with SVE who died exhibited significantly lower GCS scores and higher serum NSE concentrations compared with survivors. Neuroimaging abnormalities were also markedly more prevalent among non-survivors. These observations align with prior reports demonstrating that the magnitude of brain injury reflected by GCS, NSE, and neuroimaging is tightly associated with prognosis in viral encephalitis (7, 17). Pratamastuti D et al. found that the median serum NSE level in the acute encephalitis syndrome was significantly higher than that of the non-acute encephalitis syndrome group, these results indicate that serum NSE was a good indicator of neuronal brain injury (18). Similarly, in our study, serum NSE levels were higher in children with SVE than in those with mild viral encephalitis, and elevated serum NSE was identified as an exploratory factor associated with in-hospital mortality. Abnormal EEG and neuroimaging findings, as well as high NSE levels, reflect the extent of brain tissue injury and help assess patient prognosis.In the present study, most children with SVE received combined corticosteroid and immunoglobulin therapy, and the overall recovery rate was relatively high. In this cohort, immunomodulatory therapy was more frequently used in patients with more severe clinical presentations. The observational nature precludes causal inference, but our data provide a real-world snapshot of current management practices for pediatric SVE. In recent years, researchers have increasingly focused on exploring prognosis-associated factors in patients with established SVE, attempting to construct prediction models using clinical symptoms, laboratory indicators, and other parameters (16, 19). Gao et al. found that convulsive status epilepticus, stress-induced hyperglycemia, and miR-125b are exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE (20). Song et al. reported that levels of soluble interleukin-2 receptor (SIL-2R), endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), and CD93 in CSF and serum are significantly elevated in children with viral encephalitis and are closely associated with disease progression and prognosis, suggesting their potential value as early warning biomarkers (21). However, current research in this field is still in a preliminary stage, and a unified early warning indicator system with standardized cutoff values has not yet been established, limiting its clinical application and generalization. The key challenge in the clinical management of SVE is the mismatch between the therapeutic time window and the assessment of disease severity. This study demonstrated that seizures, EEG abnormalities, neuroimaging abnormalities, low GCS score, and elevated serum NSE level were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE. However, due to the small sample size (particularly the small number of deaths, n = 4), we were unable to perform multivariable adjustment for potential confounders. Therefore, these associations should be regarded as exploratory and preliminary rather than confirmatory. The extremely wide confidence intervals for categorical variables further reflect the statistical instability inherent in small-sample analyses. Larger multicenter studies with sufficient sample sizes are urgently needed to establish independent exploratory factors and to develop reliable risk stratification tools for pediatric SVE.Treatment modalities for SVE include antiviral drugs, osmotic agents to reduce intracranial pressure, corticosteroid and immunoglobulins, antiepileptic drugs, brain protection, and brain metabolism-enhancing agents. Studies have reported that early use of hemoperfusion combined with continuous veno-venous hemodiafiltration may improve the prognosis of pediatric SVE more than hemoperfusion alone (22). The timing of therapy initiation was within 24–48 h of diagnosis, and the indications were based on clinical judgment (rapid neurological deterioration, brain edema on imaging, or refractory seizures). In this cohort, the majority of SVE patients received corticosteroids and/or IVIG, and 84% survived to discharge. However, the observational nature of this study precludes causal inference regarding treatment efficacy. Treatment allocation was based on clinical judgment and disease severity, and differences in treatment between survivors and non-survivors likely reflect confounding by indication. Therefore, the observed association between immunotherapy and survival should not be interpreted as evidence of treatment benefit. Prospective randomized studies are needed to evaluate the efficacy of immunomodulatory therapies in pediatric SVE. The role of immunotherapy in pediatric SVE remains an area of ongoing investigation (23).Several limitations of this study must be acknowledged. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionThe burden of pediatric SVE remains substantial. Early clinical symptoms are non-specific; specific clinical markers and sensitive early-warning tools are lacking, and clinical prognosis is often unfavorable. Convulsive seizures, abnormal EEG findings, neuroimaging abnormalities, elevated serum NSE concentrations, and low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores represent potential factors associated with in-hospital mortality and merit further validation for mortality-risk stratification among children with SVE. Based on the above background, this study describes the clinical characteristics (including demographics, symptoms, signs, laboratory findings, EEG and neuroimaging features) of children with SVE in Anqing City of China, and compares the clinical and laboratory profiles between SVE and mild viral encephalitis. Finally, we identified potential factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE using univariate analysis. The ultimate goal is to provide preliminary regional data that may help clinicians recognize SVE early and guide risk stratification, while acknowledging the exploratory nature of the findings.

full_text: BackgroundThe epidemiology of pediatric acute respiratory infections (ARIs) changed substantially during the COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) pandemic, largely because of school closures, masking, reduced travel, and other non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). However, hospital-based data from the restriction period remain useful for describing pathogen detection patterns, clinical severity, and markers of adverse clinical course.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective hospital-based study of 62 children aged <18 years who were evaluated for ARI symptoms and underwent real-time fluorescent quantitative nucleic acid testing for common respiratory pathogens, including respiratory viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, severity, and outcome variables were extracted from medical records. Continuous variables were summarized using medians and ranges, and group comparisons used non-parametric tests. Given the small sample size and sparse severe-outcome events, the study was not powered to detect small effect sizes, and regression findings were interpreted conservatively as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.ResultsThe median age was 9 years (range, 1–17), and 33 patients (53.2%) were female. Most children had mild disease (37/62, 59.7%); 19 (30.6%) had moderate disease and 6 (9.7%) had severe disease. Intensive care unit (ICU) admission was recorded in 6 patients (9.7%), and mechanical ventilatory or noninvasive respiratory support in 9 (14.5%). Fever (43.5%) and cough (22.6%) were the most frequent presenting symptoms. Median oxygen saturation was 94.7% (range, 87.2–97.8). Respiratory virus detection was documented in 15 children (24.2%). Human rhinovirus was detected in 15 children (24.2%), human bocavirus in 9 (14.5%), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae in 10 (16.1%); co-detection was recorded in 14 children (22.6%). Lower SpO2 and longer symptom duration differed significantly across severity categories (both p < 0.001). full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundThe epidemiology of pediatric acute respiratory infections (ARIs) changed substantially during the COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) pandemic, largely because of school closures, masking, reduced travel, and other non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs). However, hospital-based data from the restriction period remain useful for describing pathogen detection patterns, clinical severity, and markers of adverse clinical course.MethodsWe conducted a retrospective hospital-based study of 62 children aged <18 years who were evaluated for ARI symptoms and underwent real-time fluorescent quantitative nucleic acid testing for common respiratory pathogens, including respiratory viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, severity, and outcome variables were extracted from medical records. Continuous variables were summarized using medians and ranges, and group comparisons used non-parametric tests. Given the small sample size and sparse severe-outcome events, the study was not powered to detect small effect sizes, and regression findings were interpreted conservatively as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.ResultsThe median age was 9 years (range, 1–17), and 33 patients (53.2%) were female. Most children had mild disease (37/62, 59.7%); 19 (30.6%) had moderate disease and 6 (9.7%) had severe disease. Intensive care unit (ICU) admission was recorded in 6 patients (9.7%), and mechanical ventilatory or noninvasive respiratory support in 9 (14.5%). Fever (43.5%) and cough (22.6%) were the most frequent presenting symptoms. Median oxygen saturation was 94.7% (range, 87.2–97.8). Respiratory virus detection was documented in 15 children (24.2%). Human rhinovirus was detected in 15 children (24.2%), human bocavirus in 9 (14.5%), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae in 10 (16.1%); co-detection was recorded in 14 children (22.6%). Lower SpO2 and longer symptom duration differed significantly across severity categories (both p < 0.001). In exploratory logistic regression, each additional day of symptoms was associated with higher odds of hospital admission/continued inpatient management [odds ratio [OR], 1.4; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03–1.93; p = 0.022]. Sex was not significantly associated with clinical severity or laboratory parameters.ConclusionsIn this small hospital-based pediatric ARI cohort during the COVID-19 restriction period, severe disease was uncommon, and oxygen saturation and symptom duration were the most clinically coherent markers of greater severity. The observed pathogen detection pattern is compatible with pandemic-era disruption of respiratory pathogen circulation, but causal conclusions about NPIs require larger denominator-based studies with pre-pandemic and post-restriction comparison groups.

full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionIn this retrospective hospital-based study of 62 children with ARIs evaluated during the COVID-19 restriction period, most cases were mild, severe disease was uncommon, and ICU admission occurred in fewer than 10% of children. The most coherent clinical severity markers were lower oxygen saturation and longer symptom duration. Respiratory virus detection was documented in approximately one quarter of children, with rhinovirus being the most frequently detected virus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae detected in a smaller but clinically relevant proportion. Co-detection occurred in more than one fifth of the cohort.The finding that low SpO2 tracked with disease severity is clinically expected and strengthens internal validity. Oxygen saturation is an objective bedside indicator of lower respiratory tract involvement and impaired gas exchange. This pattern is consistent with prior pediatric respiratory cohorts in which oxygen saturation and other clinical features tracked with severity, although such bedside features alone have limited ability to identify the causative pathogen (15). Similarly, longer symptom duration may indicate delayed presentation, progressive disease, treatment failure, or more persistent infection, explaining its association with admission/continued inpatient management. Comparable associations between prolonged symptom duration and hospital-based management have been reported in rhinovirus-associated pediatric acute respiratory infection (16). These findings support prioritizing oxygen saturation and symptom trajectory in triage and follow-up decisions for pediatric ARIs.The pathogen profile should be interpreted in the context of pandemic-era transmission disruption. Multiple studies from China and other settings have reported altered circulation, reduced activity, or delayed resurgence of several pediatric respiratory pathogens during and after COVID-19 restrictions. In mainland China, detection rates for common respiratory viruses declined during periods of strict NPIs and rebounded after restrictions were relaxed, with earlier and more pronounced rhinovirus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae activity reported in several post-restriction cohorts (5, 9, 10, 17–19). Comparable patterns of viral suppression followed by resurgence have also been described in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and other East Asian settings (6–8, 20). However, the present dataset cannot directly estimate the population prevalence of ARIs or quantify the independent effect of NPIs because it lacks a denominator, a pre-pandemic comparator group, and post-restriction follow-up. Therefore, the current results are best framed as a hospital-based description of ARI cases and pathogen detection during 2020–2021 rather than as evidence of NPI efficacy by themselves.The relative predominance of rhinovirus in this cohort is biologically plausible. As a non-enveloped virus, rhinovirus is comparatively resistant to environmental degradation and to some hygiene-based interventions that primarily disrupt transmission of enveloped viruses such as influenza and respiratory syncytial virus, which may explain its continued circulation when other pathogens were suppressed (3, 21). Co-detection of rhinovirus with other respiratory pathogens is also frequently reported in pediatric cohorts and does not necessarily indicate greater severity, consistent with the absence of a significant association between virus detection and severity category in the present data (16, 21–23). Mycoplasma pneumoniae follows a multi-year epidemic cycle of approximately 3–7 years that is thought to reflect population immunity dynamics rather than short-term public health measures; detection of Mycoplasma pneumoniae in this cohort during the restriction period is therefore compatible with its intrinsic epidemic periodicity rather than a specific NPI-related effect (5, 24–26).The high rate of antibiotic use deserves careful interpretation. Antibiotics were prescribed in three quarters of children despite respiratory virus detection in a minority and low median procalcitonin. This pattern may reflect empirical management during diagnostic uncertainty, concern for atypical pathogens such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, local protocols, or severity-based treatment decisions. This proportion exceeds the confirmed bacterial or atypical-pathogen detection rate in this cohort and mirrors a broader pattern of empirical antibiotic use described in other pandemic-era pediatric respiratory cohorts (9, 19). Future studies should evaluate antimicrobial stewardship indicators, bacterial culture results, radiological findings, and outcomes to distinguish appropriate empirical therapy from potentially avoidable antibiotic exposure.The absence of significant sex-based differences suggests that sex was not a major determinant of laboratory findings or clinical course in this small cohort. Although the original ordinal model produced a numerically higher odds ratio for female sex, this was not statistically significant and should not be interpreted as evidence of sex-related severity differences. This null finding is consistent with most pediatric ARI cohorts, in which sex has not emerged as a consistent independent predictor of severity (24, 27). Broader demographic and clinical characteristics nonetheless remain relevant to the risk and clinical presentation of respiratory infections in paediatric patients (28).4.1Strengths and limitationsThis study provides real-world hospital-based data during a unique period of respiratory pathogen disruption. It includes demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, pathogen-detection, severity, and outcome data, allowing integrated description of clinical phenotype and severity markers.Important limitations must be acknowledged. First, the sample size was small, and only six severe cases were recorded; therefore, multivariable models are exploratory and at risk of overfitting. Second, the single-center retrospective design limits generalizability and may introduce selection, documentation, and testing biases, including selection bias from physician-discretion pathogen testing rather than universal screening, which may have enriched the tested sample for more symptomatic or severe presentations. Third, the dataset does not include a population denominator, pre-pandemic comparison group, or post-restriction group, preventing true prevalence estimation and causal inference about NPIs. Fourth, the dataset did not include SARS-CoV-2 co-testing status, a validated disease-severity scoring instrument, radiological findings, or blood culture results, which limits assessment of SARS-CoV-2 co-infection and of relative bacterial versus viral contributions to severity. Fifth, because hospital admission/continued inpatient management was defined broadly to include continued observation beyond initial emergency evaluation (Methods), the low proportion of children with formal ward admission reflects this definition and should not be read as indicating a non-hospital-based sample. Finally, sparse-outcome regression for prognosis produced unstable estimates and was not suitable for primary interpretation; future analyses of similarly small, sparse-event pediatric ARI datasets may benefit from penalized regression approaches, such as Firth's correction, to reduce small-sample bias (29). Because mechanical ventilatory/noninvasive respiratory support was captured as a separate variable from formal admission status, these counts should not be assumed to be nested, and readers should refer to the Definitions subsection when comparing the two.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionAmong children with ARIs evaluated during the COVID-19 restriction period, most cases were mild and severe disease was infrequent. Lower oxygen saturation and longer symptom duration were the most clinically meaningful markers of greater severity and admission/continued inpatient management. Respiratory virus detection, especially rhinovirus, and pathogen co-detection were observed, but the study should be interpreted as a hospital-based clinical description rather than a denominator-based prevalence analysis. Larger multicenter studies with pre-pandemic, restriction-period, and post-restriction comparison groups are needed to clarify the long-term effects of pandemic control measures on pediatric respiratory pathogen epidemiology and clinical outcomes.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionAcute respiratory infections (ARIs) remain among the most frequent causes of pediatric illness, health-care use, antimicrobial exposure, and hospitalization worldwide (1). Their clinical spectrum ranges from self-limited upper respiratory tract infections to severe lower respiratory tract disease, respiratory failure, and death, particularly among young children, children with comorbidities, and populations with limited access to timely care (2).Pediatric ARIs are etiologically heterogeneous. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), rhinovirus/enterovirus, influenza viruses, parainfluenza viruses, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, human bocavirus, seasonal coronaviruses, atypical bacteria such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and bacterial pathogens may produce overlapping clinical syndromes (3, 4). Because fever, cough, dyspnea, and inflammatory markers are not sufficiently pathogen-specific, laboratory testing is often required to characterize etiology and guide infection-control and antimicrobial decisions (5).The COVID-19 pandemic created an unusual natural experiment in respiratory pathogen transmission. Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), including masking, hand hygiene, school closures, travel restrictions, isolation policies, and reduced social mixing, were associated in many settings with reduced circulation of several non-SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) respiratory viruses (6–8). Subsequent relaxation of restrictions was followed by altered seasonality and resurgence of pathogens such as RSV, influenza, rhinovirus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae in several pediatric cohorts (9–11).For small hospital-based datasets collected during the restriction period, the strongest contribution is not estimation of population prevalence or causal attribution to NPIs, but careful description of clinical patterns, pathogen detection, and severity markers (12). Such data can help hospitals interpret pandemic-era case mix, identify simple bedside indicators of severity, and design larger surveillance studies.Therefore, this study aimed to describe the demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, and pathogen-detection characteristics of children evaluated for ARIs during 2020–2021, and to explore clinical markers associated with disease severity, hospital admission/continued inpatient management, and prognosis. 2.2ParticipantsEligible participants were children aged <18 years with symptoms compatible with ARI, including fever, cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea, dyspnea, or shortness of breath, who underwent respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing during the study period. A total of 96 children with ARI-compatible presentations were initially screened during 2020–2021. Exclusion criteria were: duplicate encounters for the same illness episode, incomplete core clinical records, or absence of respiratory pathogen test results. Applying these criteria led to exclusion of 34 children (12 duplicate encounters, 15 with incomplete core clinical records, and 7 without respiratory pathogen test results). The final analytic sample included 62 children. Because respiratory pathogen testing was ordered at the treating physician's discretion rather than through universal screening, children with more severe or prolonged symptoms may have been preferentially tested, and this selection pattern should be considered when interpreting pathogen-detection frequencies and their association with severity. The participant-selection process is summarized in the flow diagram (Figure 1).Figure 1Participant selection flow diagram showing the number of children screened for eligibility, excluded (with reasons), and included in the final analytic sample.Flowchart showing selection of children with acute respiratory infection-compatible presentations screened between 2020 and 2021, with n equal to ninety-six initially screened, thirty-four excluded for reasons listed, and sixty-two in the final analytic sample with respiratory pathogen testing. 2.3Data collectionDemographic and clinical data were extracted from charts and electronic medical records by trained reviewers. Variables included age, sex, body weight, height, body mass index (BMI), symptom type and duration, oxygen saturation (SpO2), hospital admission/continued inpatient management, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, mechanical ventilation/noninvasive respiratory support, length of hospital and ICU stay, white blood cell count (WBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, pathogen test results, co-detection, antiviral therapy, antibiotic therapy, corticosteroid use, supportive treatment, severity classification, and clinical outcome. Personal identifiers were coded before analysis. 2.4Pathogen testingRespiratory specimens were tested using real-time fluorescent quantitative PCR (polymerase chain reaction) assays for common respiratory viruses and Mycoplasma pneumoniae RNA/DNA. Nasopharyngeal swab specimens were collected within 24 h of presentation and processed in the hospital's clinical microbiology laboratory using a multiplex respiratory pathogen panel targeting influenza A and B viruses, respiratory syncytial virus, human rhinovirus, human bocavirus, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza viruses 1–3, adenovirus, seasonal coronaviruses, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Each assay run included a positive control, a negative (no-template) control, and an internal amplification control to monitor extraction and amplification efficiency, following the reagent manufacturer's instructions and routine laboratory quality-assurance procedures. A specimen was classified as positive for a given pathogen when the cycle-threshold value was below the manufacturer-specified cutoff with a typical sigmoidal amplification curve and a valid internal control; results with an invalid internal control or atypical amplification curve were repeated before being reported. 2.5DefinitionsARI was defined clinically by compatible acute respiratory symptoms. Severity was categorized as mild, moderate, or severe. Co-detection was defined as detection of more than one respiratory pathogen in the same illness episode. Clinical outcome was categorized as recovery, complication, or death according to discharge records. Hospital admission/continued inpatient management was defined as continued observation and treatment beyond the initial emergency evaluation, consistent with the emergency-department-based case mix of this cohort, in which most children were evaluated, treated, and discharged without formal ward admission. Mechanical ventilatory/noninvasive respiratory support was recorded independently of formal admission status and could be provided during emergency-department management; therefore, the number of children receiving such support does not necessarily correspond to the number meeting admission criteria. 2.6Ethical considerationsThe study was approved by the Ethics Committee. Because this was a retrospective analysis of de-identified records, the requirement for individual informed consent was waived. 2.7Statistical analysisContinuous variables were summarized using medians and ranges because the distributions were non-normal and the sample was small. Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Sex-based and pathogen-detection group comparisons were performed using Mann–Whitney U tests for continuous variables and Fisher exact or chi-square tests for categorical variables as appropriate. Comparisons across severity categories used Kruskal–Wallis tests with post-hoc pairwise comparisons when the global test was significant. Binary logistic regression was used exploratorily to assess predictors of hospital admission/continued inpatient management. Ordinal logistic regression was used exploratorily for severity. Candidate predictors for the multivariable models (age, sex, weight, SpO2, and duration of symptoms) were selected a priori on the basis of clinical plausibility and were retained for…

title_original: Clinical characteristics, pathogen detection, and severity markers among children with acute respiratory infections during the COVID-19 restriction period: a retrospective hospital-based study

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the clinical characteristics, pathogen detection, and severity markers of acute respiratory infections (ARIs) in children during the COVID-19 restriction period in China, to better understand the impact of these restrictions on respiratory virus epidemiology and clinical outcomes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This was a retrospective hospital-based study conducted in China from January 2020 to December 2021, involving 62 children with ARIs who had available pathogen testing results. The study focused on those evaluated during the period of strict public health measures related to the pandemic.
analysis.methods: The study extracted demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment, severity, and outcome variables from medical records. It applied exclusion criteria to remove duplicate encounters, incomplete records, and cases without respiratory pathogen test results. The study was not powered to detect small effect sizes and used exploratory logistic regression to analyze associations between symptom duration and hospital admission.
analysis.main_results: The median age was 9 years (range, 1–17), and 33 children (53.2%) were female. Fever was the most common presenting symptom (43.5%), followed by cough alone (22.6%), with 19.4% having both fever and cough. Respiratory virus detection was recorded in 15 children (24.2%), with human rhinovirus being the most frequent (24.2%), followed by human bocavirus (14.5%) and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (16.1%). Co-detection was observed in 14 children (22.6%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that respiratory virus detection was common but varied in frequency, with human rhinovirus being the most frequently detected virus. They noted that Mycoplasma pneumoniae was detected in a smaller but clinically relevant proportion, suggesting its potential role in disease severity.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the epidemiology and clinical manifestations of respiratory viruses in children during the pandemic, which can inform surveillance strategies and public health measures aimed at mitigating the spread of these pathogens.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by its small sample size and sparse severe-outcome events, which reduced its power to detect small effect sizes. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of randomized or controlled components.

analysis.summary_en: This retrospective hospital-based study analyzed clinical characteristics, pathogen detection, and severity markers of acute respiratory infections (ARIs) in 62 children in China during the COVID-19 restriction period. The median age was 9 years, with 53.2% female. Fever was the most common symptom, followed by cough. Respiratory viruses were detected in 24.2% of children, with human rhinovirus being the most frequent. Mycoplasma pneumoniae was detected in 16.1% of cases, and co-detection was observed in 22.6% of children. Most cases were mild, with only 9.7% requiring ICU admission. The study highlights the impact of pandemic restrictions on respiratory virus circulation and clinical outcomes, but its moderate evidence strength is limited by the small sample size and lack of power to detect small effects.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查中国COVID-19限制期间儿童急性呼吸道感染(ARIs)的临床特征、病原体检测和严重程度标志物,以更好地了解这些限制对呼吸道病毒流行病学和临床结果的影响。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这是一项 2020 年 1 月至 2021 年 12 月在中国进行的回顾性医院研究,涉及 62 名具有可用病原体检测结果的 ARI 儿童。该研究的重点是在与大流行相关的严格公共卫生措施期间进行评估的人员。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究从医疗记录中提取了人口统计、临床、实验室、治疗、严重程度和结果变量。它应用排除标准来消除重复遭遇、不完整记录和没有呼吸道病原体检测结果的病例。该研究无法检测小效应大小,并使用探索性逻辑回归来分析症状持续时间与入院之间的关联。
elements_zh.main_results: 中位年龄为 9 岁(范围为 1-17 岁),其中 33 名儿童 (53.2%) 为女性。发烧是最常见的症状(43.5%),其次是咳嗽(22.6%),19.4%的人同时发烧和咳嗽。15名儿童(24.2%)检测到呼吸道病毒,其中最常见的是人鼻病毒(24.2%),其次是人博卡病毒(14.5%)和肺炎支原体(16.1%)。在 14 名儿童(22.6%)中观察到了共同检测。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,呼吸道病毒检测很常见,但频率各不相同,其中人鼻病毒是最常检测到的病毒。他们指出,检测到的肺炎支原体比例较小,但与临床相关,这表明其在疾病严重程度中具有潜在作用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现提供了对大流行期间儿童呼吸道病毒 流行病学 和临床表现的深入了解,这可以为旨在减轻这些病原体传播的 监测 策略和公共卫生措施提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到样本量小和严重后果事件稀疏的限制,从而降低了检测小效应大小的能力。由于该研究的观察性质以及缺乏随机或对照成分,证据是中等的。
